title: McKenna v. Vernon
summary: An owner who repeatedly paid without the architect’s required certificate could not invoke the absent final certificate to defeat payment for honestly and substantially completed work.
notes: The case is McKenna v. Vernon, 258 Pa. 18, 101 A. 919 (1917); the builder sued for the $2,750 balance (recovering $2,500), and the architect testified that the theatre was substantially completed and that he withheld certificates only because no one asked him for them.

sections.Parties: McKenna was the builder of a moving-picture theatre. Vernon was the owner required to make progress and final payments.
sections.Material Facts:
The theatre contract price was $8,750. The first eighty percent was payable in installments, with final payment within thirty days after completion. Each payment was conditioned on the architect’s certificate.

Vernon made seven payments totaling $6,000; all but one were made without requesting a certificate. He observed the work almost daily without contemporaneous objection to its materials or execution. When the builder sued for the remainder, Vernon alleged defects. The architect testified that there had been no unauthorized departures from the specifications. Vernon then argued that the absence of a final certificate prevented the action.
sections.Procedural History: McKenna obtained a $2,500 judgment. Vernon appealed on the certificate condition. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court affirmed.
sections.Issue: Could Vernon insist on a final certificate after repeatedly disregarding the same certificate requirement while the work progressed?
sections.Holding: On these facts the certificate requirement was waived, and its absence did not bar recovery.
sections.Reasoning:
The repeated course of payment showed that the owner had not been insisting on the formal condition. His ongoing observation without complaint reinforced the conclusion that he could not resurrect the requirement at the end to defeat payment for honest and substantial performance.

The waiver concerned the certificate condition. It did not establish that every instance of lenience forever eliminates a payment or quality requirement. The accompanying discussion asks how a party might reinstate a waived requirement prospectively and contrasts temporary indulgence with an indefinite commitment to forbear.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Conduct during performance can change whether a party may insist on a condition, even though the written contract originally required it.

topics.waiver: Repeated payment without certificates supported waiver of the certificate condition.
topics.conditions: The issue concerned excuse of a condition to payment.
topics.interpretation: The parties’ performance matters to the legal treatment of the written requirement.
topics.assent: A course of conduct may show that a party has relinquished insistence on a contractual condition.
topics.express-conditions: The architect's certificate was an express condition to each payment, which is the requirement the owner's conduct waived.
topics.substantial-performance: The architect testified that the theatre was substantially completed, which underlies the court's refusal to let the missing certificate defeat payment.
